- architecture-09 | architecture | senior | single | Which statement correctly distinguishes domain events from integration events? | Domain events are handled in-process within the same bounded context, typically as part of the same transaction, while integration events notify other bounded contexts or services and must be published only after the transaction commits.
- architecture-10 | architecture | senior | open | Sales, Support and Billing all use the word 'Customer' with different attributes and rules; should the system have one shared Customer model, and what is the alternative? | Each bounded context should own its own Customer model expressed in its ubiquitous language, linked by identity and translated at the boundaries, because one canonical model couples all contexts and grows inconsistent.
- architecture-11 | architecture | lead | open | How would you keep the modules of a .NET modular monolith from silently coupling to each other as the team grows? | Boundaries must be enforced mechanically, not by convention: a public contract per module with internal implementation types, data owned per module (separate schema, no cross-module joins), and automated architecture tests in CI that fail on forbidden references.
- architecture-12 | architecture | lead | situation | Your team proposes splitting the monolith into microservices because builds are slow and merge conflicts are frequent; how do you decide and what do you propose? | Slow builds and merge conflicts are solved by modularising the codebase and the build, not by distribution; extract a service only for a concrete need such as independent scaling, deployment cadence or team ownership, after module boundaries have proven stable.
- architecture-13 | architecture | lead | situation | A company template forces every new service into four projects with a mediator handler per endpoint, and a small internal CRUD service is taking weeks; what do you decide and how do you handle the template owners? | Architecture should match domain complexity: a simple CRUD service warrants a lighter structure, while the decision is agreed and documented with the template owners, keeping a clear path to add layers if the domain grows.
- architecture-14 | architecture | architect | open | How does Conway's law affect where service and module boundaries end up, and how can an architect use it deliberately? | Systems mirror the communication structure of the organisation, so boundaries that cut across team ownership create constant cross-team coordination; aligning teams with bounded contexts (the inverse Conway manoeuvre) makes the intended architecture stable.
- architecture-15 | architecture | architect | open | Should every bounded context become exactly one microservice, and what goes wrong when a service spans several contexts or a context is split into many tiny services? | A bounded context is a natural upper bound for a service: a service spanning contexts mixes models and owners, while splitting a context into many services turns in-context transactions into chatty cross-service calls; split further only for concrete scaling or deployment reasons.
- architecture-16 | architecture | architect | single | Two microservices read and write the same tables in one database; what is the main architectural cost of this arrangement? | Sharing tables couples the services through the schema, so neither can change its data model or deploy independently; each microservice should own its data and expose it only through its API or events.
- architecture-17 | architecture | architect | multi | Select the capabilities an organisation should have in place before adopting microservices, from a list mixing operational prerequisites with optional technologies such as event sourcing, Kubernetes or a different language per service. | Fowler's prerequisites are operational: rapid provisioning, basic monitoring and rapid automated deployment; specific platforms, event sourcing or polyglot languages are not prerequisites.
- architecture-18 | architecture | architect | situation | A large .NET Framework monolith must be moved to a modern architecture without a feature freeze or a big-bang rewrite; outline your migration approach. | Migrate incrementally with the strangler fig pattern: put a routing facade in front, carve out one capability at a time behind an anti-corruption layer that shields the new model from the legacy one, and retire legacy parts only once traffic has moved.
- distributed-01 | distributed | junior | single | Three instances of a service read from one point-to-point queue; the question asks how many of them process each message, compared with three subscribers of a publish-subscribe topic. | With competing consumers on one queue each message is delivered to exactly one consumer, while publish-subscribe gives every subscription its own copy.
- distributed-02 | distributed | middle | single | A RabbitMQ consumer uses automatic acknowledgement and crashes halfway through a message; the question asks what happens to that message and to the messages already prefetched. | With automatic acknowledgement the broker treats a message as delivered once it is sent, so a consumer crash loses it; manual ack after processing makes the broker redeliver it.
- distributed-03 | distributed | middle | single | Events of one order must be consumed in the order they were produced from a topic with 12 partitions; the question asks which producer setting guarantees that. | Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so all events of one order must use the same message key (for example the order id) to land in the same partition.
- distributed-04 | distributed | middle | find-bug | A BCL-only simulation of a message consumer records the message id in a processed set before crediting an account; the credit fails once, the message is redelivered and skipped, and the program prints a balance of 0 instead of 100. | The message id must be recorded only together with (or after) a successful side effect, otherwise a failure after marking turns a redelivery into a silently lost message.
- distributed-05 | distributed | middle | multi | Select every situation that makes a consumer receive the same message twice under at-least-once delivery: a crash after the database commit but before the ack, a producer resending after a lost publisher confirm, a Kafka rebalance before the offset commit, versus a durable write to disk or a message TTL expiry. | Duplicates arise whenever processing or storage succeeded but the confirmation of it (ack, publisher confirm, offset commit) was lost, so the sender or broker repeats the delivery.
- distributed-06 | distributed | senior | find-bug | A BCL-only simulation of an outbox relay removes a row from the outbox list and then calls a fake broker whose first publish throws; the next relay pass finds an empty outbox and the program prints that 0 messages were published. | The relay must delete or mark an outbox row only after the broker confirmed the publish, accepting at-least-once delivery instead of losing the message.
- distributed-07 | distributed | senior | open | A handler saves an order with EF Core and then publishes an OrderCreated event to the broker; the question asks what can go wrong in this sequence and how the transactional outbox fixes it. | There is no atomic transaction spanning the database and the broker, so either write can succeed alone; the outbox stores the event in the same local transaction as the data and a relay publishes it afterwards at least once.
- distributed-08 | distributed | senior | multi | Select every sound practice for retrying failed calls from a message consumer to a downstream service: exponential backoff, random jitter, a bounded number of attempts, retrying only transient errors, versus immediate tight-loop retries and independent retries at every layer of the call chain. | Retries must be bounded, spaced with growing randomized delays and limited to transient faults, because unbounded, synchronized or stacked retries multiply load on a service that is already failing.
- distributed-09 | distributed | senior | situation | One malformed message makes the consumer throw on every delivery, it is redelivered endlessly, the queue backlog grows and the logs fill with the same stack trace; the question asks what to do now and what to change. | Cap delivery attempts and move the failing message to a dead-letter queue with its error, alert on dead-letter depth, then fix the bug and replay the dead-lettered messages deliberately.
- distributed-10 | distributed | senior | single | A consumer group on a 6-partition topic lags under load and the team scales it from 6 to 12 instances; the question asks what effect this has on throughput. | Each partition is assigned to at most one consumer in a group, so instances beyond the partition count stay idle; throughput needs more partitions, which also remaps keys and breaks per-key ordering during the change.
- distributed-11 | distributed | lead | open | The team must pick one broker for a new platform that needs both background job queues and an event stream other teams will read; the question asks how you decide between Kafka and RabbitMQ and what risks you weigh. | Kafka is a partitioned, retained log that consumers can replay at their own offsets, while RabbitMQ routes messages and deletes them after per-message acknowledgement; the choice follows replay and fan-out needs versus routing and task-queue semantics, plus the team's ability to operate it.
- distributed-12 | distributed | lead | situation | After a broker failover dozens of customers were charged twice because payment commands were redelivered; the question asks how you lead the response and what you change so it cannot recur. | Contain and refund first, then make the payment step idempotent end to end with a stable idempotency key passed to the payment provider and a reconciliation job, rather than relying on the broker to deliver exactly once.
- distributed-13 | distributed | architect | open | An order flow spans payment, inventory, shipping and loyalty services; the question asks when you would coordinate it with choreography through events and when with a central orchestrator. | Choreography keeps services decoupled and suits a few steps, but as steps grow the flow becomes implicit and hard to trace; an orchestrator makes the flow and compensations explicit at the cost of a central component that knows every participant.
- distributed-14 | distributed | architect | multi | Select every true statement about saga compensations: they are new business actions rather than database rollbacks, they must be idempotent and retryable, other transactions can see intermediate states, versus claims that a saga gives ACID isolation or that compensation restores the exact previous state. | A saga is a sequence of local commits, so it lacks isolation and compensations are semantic undo operations that must tolerate retries and may not restore the original state exactly.
- distributed-15 | distributed | architect | open | A team says Kafka's exactly-once semantics mean their consumers that write to SQL Server and call a payment API need no deduplication; the question asks whether that is true and what end-to-end guarantee you can actually design for. | Kafka transactions give exactly-once only for read-process-write within Kafka; any side effect in an external system still sees at-least-once delivery, so effectively-once comes from idempotent processing or storing offsets atomically with the result.
- distributed-16 | distributed | architect | open | In a system of order, inventory and billing services the question asks how you decide which invariants must be strongly consistent and which may become consistent eventually, and what the business must accept for the latter. | Invariants that must never be violated even briefly belong inside one service's local transaction boundary; rules that span services are made eventually consistent through events, sagas and reconciliation, trading immediate correctness for availability and latency.
- system-design-01 | system-design | middle | single | In the cache-aside pattern, what should the service do with the cached entry when it updates the record in the database? | Write to the database first and then remove the cache entry, so the next read reloads fresh data; writing the new value into the cache instead races with concurrent readers and can leave a stale value.
- system-design-02 | system-design | middle | multi | Before running an ASP.NET Core app as several instances behind a load balancer, which kinds of state must be moved out of the process or local machine? | Anything one instance writes and another must read: the Data Protection key ring, session data in an in-memory store, authoritative values held only in IMemoryCache and files saved to local disk; stateless singletons and read-only configuration need no change.
- system-design-03 | system-design | middle | open | When is scaling a service vertically a better choice than scaling it horizontally, and what does horizontal scaling require from the design? | Scaling up is simpler and needs no design changes but hits a hardware ceiling and keeps a single point of failure; scaling out needs stateless, partitionable work and a load balancer but grows almost linearly and adds redundancy.
- system-design-04 | system-design | senior | situation | Every few minutes the database CPU spikes to 100% at the moment a popular cached product list expires; what do you do? | Many concurrent misses on one hot key all hit the database at once, so the fix is to coalesce requests per key (for example HybridCache stampede protection in .NET 9), refresh before expiry and add jitter to expiration times.
- system-design-05 | system-design | senior | single | Why is an auto-incrementing order id or a creation timestamp a poor key for range-based sharding of a write-heavy orders table? | Monotonic keys send every new write to the last range, so one shard takes all inserts while the others idle; a key with even distribution, such as a hash, spreads the writes.
- system-design-06 | system-design | senior | open | A team configures the ASP.NET Core rate limiting middleware (.NET 7 and later) at 100 requests per minute per client and then scales the API to 6 instances; what limit do clients actually get and how would you enforce a global one? | The built-in limiters keep counters in each process, so the effective limit grows with the instance count (up to 600 per minute); a global limit needs a shared counter store or enforcement at a gateway in front of the instances.
- system-design-07 | system-design | senior | situation | You are asked to size a photo-sharing service with 10 million daily users, each uploading 2 photos and viewing 50 per day; how do you estimate request rates, storage and bandwidth before choosing components? | Convert daily volumes to average and peak requests per second (daily count / 86400 times a peak factor), multiply writes by object size and retention for storage, and use the 25:1 read/write ratio to justify caching and a CDN for reads.
- system-design-08 | system-design | lead | situation | Two weeks before a release a developer proposes adding a Redis cache to fix a slow endpoint; as the tech lead, how do you decide whether to accept it? | A cache adds a second source of truth and a new production dependency, so accept it only after measuring where the time goes, confirming the read/write ratio and acceptable staleness, and agreeing who owns invalidation, monitoring and the failure mode when the cache is down.
- system-design-09 | system-design | lead | open | Before your team starts designing a new service, which non-functional requirements do you insist on clarifying with stakeholders and why? | Availability and latency targets, expected load and growth, read/write ratio, data consistency and retention needs and cost limits each change the architecture, so designing without them means guessing and redesigning later.
- system-design-10 | system-design | architect | situation | Traffic is expected to grow fivefold over two years and the single relational database is already the bottleneck; what sequence of steps do you plan? | Exhaust cheaper reversible options first (query and index tuning, read replicas, caching, functional partitioning by bounded data sets) and shard only when writes outgrow one server, because sharding moves joins and transactions into the application and is hard to undo.
- system-design-11 | system-design | architect | situation | The business asks for the service to survive a full region outage; how do you choose between active-passive and active-active multi-region deployment? | Active-passive is simpler but its recovery time and data loss depend on failover and replication lag, while active-active gives near-zero recovery time only if the data model tolerates concurrent writes in several regions or partitions writes by region; RTO, RPO and consistency needs decide.
- system-design-12 | system-design | architect | open | For a multi-tenant SaaS product, when would you scale by deploying independent stamps of the whole stack instead of growing one shared deployment? | Stamps cap the blast radius, give a known scale unit and allow data residency per region, at the cost of tenant routing, fleet-wide deployments and cross-stamp operations, so they pay off when one shared deployment hits scale limits or isolation requirements.
- system-design-13 | system-design | architect | situation | A news site with readers worldwide sees read traffic jump 100 times during breaking news; how do you design caching so the origin survives? | Serve most reads from the CDN edge using HTTP caching rules: long-lived versioned URLs for static assets, short shared-cache lifetimes with stale-while-revalidate for pages, so the origin sees roughly one request per object per TTL instead of one per reader.
- system-design-14 | system-design | architect | situation | Product demands 99.99% availability for a checkout flow that synchronously calls five dependencies, each offering 99.9%; what do you tell them and what do you change? | Availability of serial dependencies multiplies, so the flow tops out near 99.5%; reaching the target needs redundancy for critical dependencies, removing non-essential calls from the synchronous path with graceful degradation, or renegotiating the target.
- devops-01 | devops | junior | open | Why does a typical Dockerfile for a .NET app use a multi-stage build with the SDK image for building and the ASP.NET runtime image for the final stage? | Only the last stage becomes the shipped image, so the SDK, sources and intermediate build output stay out of it, which makes the image smaller and reduces its attack surface.
- devops-02 | devops | junior | single | Which statement correctly distinguishes continuous delivery from continuous deployment? | In continuous delivery every change is kept releasable and production release is a manual business decision, while in continuous deployment every change that passes the pipeline goes to production automatically.
- devops-03 | devops | junior | single | Which HTTP header carries the trace id and parent span id between services under the W3C Trace Context standard used by default in .NET? | The traceparent header carries the version, trace id, parent span id and trace flags; tracestate only carries vendor-specific data.
- devops-04 | devops | junior | open | What are logs, metrics and traces, and what question about a running service is each one best at answering? | Metrics are cheap aggregated numbers that show that something is wrong, traces show where in a request path across services time or errors occur, and logs give the detailed event context of why.
- devops-05 | devops | middle | find-bug | Find the line in a .NET Dockerfile that makes every source change re-run dotnet restore and download all packages again. | COPY . . placed before dotnet restore invalidates the restore layer on any file change; copying only the project files first and restoring before copying the rest keeps the restore layer cached.
- devops-06 | devops | middle | single | After moving an app to the .NET 8 ASP.NET Core container images, the orchestrator still sends traffic to port 80 and gets no answer; which port does the app listen on by default? | Starting with .NET 8 the official ASP.NET Core images set ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS to 8080 instead of listening on port 80.
- devops-07 | devops | middle | multi | Which ways of writing a log call with Microsoft.Extensions.Logging keep OrderId as a separate structured property in the log sink? | A message template with named placeholders and a [LoggerMessage] source-generated method keep structured properties, while string interpolation and concatenation bake the values into a flat message string.
- devops-08 | devops | middle | single | Which System.Diagnostics.Metrics instrument should record the duration of each processed request so that dashboards can show p95 and p99? | A Histogram records a distribution of values from which percentiles can be computed, whereas a Counter only sums and an UpDownCounter tracks a current total.
- devops-09 | devops | middle | find-bug | Find the line in BCL code using ActivitySource that throws NullReferenceException when no tracing listener is registered. | ActivitySource.StartActivity returns null when no ActivityListener samples the source, so calling SetTag on the result without a null-conditional operator throws.
- devops-10 | devops | senior | multi | Which tags are safe to attach to an HTTP request duration metric without blowing up the number of time series in the metrics backend? | Bounded values such as route template, HTTP method and status code are safe, while user id, raw URL path with ids or request id create unbounded cardinality and exhaust backend memory.
- devops-11 | devops | senior | open | When would you choose a blue-green deployment over a canary release for a high-traffic service, and what does each cost you? | Blue-green gives an instant full switch and rollback at the price of double capacity and exposing all users at once, while canary limits blast radius by gradual traffic shifting but needs per-version metrics, longer rollouts and both versions coexisting.
- devops-12 | devops | senior | situation | Tracing is configured with 1% head-based sampling and the traces of the rare failing requests you need to investigate are almost never recorded; what do you change? | Head sampling decides before the outcome is known, so keeping error and slow traces requires tail-based sampling in a collector (or a parent-based policy plus always-sampled errors) while accepting its buffering cost.
- devops-13 | devops | lead | situation | Your pipeline rebuilds the app separately for staging and production, and a production bug cannot be reproduced on staging; what process change do you drive with the team and how do you roll it out? | Build one immutable versioned artifact or image once and promote that exact artifact through environments, with environment differences supplied only by configuration, so what was tested is what ships.
- devops-14 | devops | architect | open | How do you roll out a breaking database schema change used by several independently deployed services that update with rolling deployments and no downtime? | Use expand-contract (parallel change): add the new schema alongside the old, make every service version compatible with both, migrate data, and remove the old schema only after no running version depends on it.
- ui-dotnet-01 | ui-dotnet | junior | single | When does a two-way WPF binding on TextBox.Text write the typed value back to the view model property by default? | The default UpdateSourceTrigger for TextBox.Text is LostFocus, so the source is updated when the text box loses focus, not on every keystroke, unless PropertyChanged is set explicitly.
- ui-dotnet-02 | ui-dotnet | junior | open | Why does a view model bound to WPF or MAUI controls implement INotifyPropertyChanged, and what happens on screen if it does not? | The binding engine subscribes to PropertyChanged and re-reads only the named property when the event fires; without the event a changed plain CLR property is never pushed to the bound control.
- ui-dotnet-03 | ui-dotnet | junior | single | In .NET 8 and later Blazor, where does component code execute when a component uses the InteractiveServer render mode? | With InteractiveServer the component runs on the server; browser events travel to it over a SignalR circuit and the server sends back UI diffs, whereas InteractiveWebAssembly runs the code in the browser.
- ui-dotnet-04 | ui-dotnet | junior | single | With @bind on an input element and no extra modifiers, when is the bound C# field updated as the user types? | @bind on an input uses the onchange event by default, so the field updates when the element loses focus after a change; @bind:event="oninput" is needed to update on every keystroke.
- ui-dotnet-05 | ui-dotnet | junior | multi | A list control is bound to an ObservableCollection<T> of plain item classes; which of the listed changes does the list show without any extra code? | ObservableCollection<T> raises CollectionChanged for Add, Remove, Insert and Clear, but not when a property of an existing item changes (that needs INotifyPropertyChanged on the item) or when the view model property is reassigned to a new collection without its own notification.
- ui-dotnet-06 | ui-dotnet | middle | find-bug | A runnable BCL view model with a subscriber that prints received property names raises PropertyChanged with a copy-pasted string name in one setter, so the change of that property is never reported; find the line. | The binding engine matches the event by property name, so a setter that raises PropertyChanged with another property's name leaves its own bindings stale; nameof or [CallerMemberName] prevents the mismatch.
- ui-dotnet-07 | ui-dotnet | middle | find-bug | A Blazor component updates a counter in a System.Threading.Timer callback and calls StateHasChanged directly; find the line that fails at run time. | A timer callback runs outside the renderer's dispatcher, so StateHasChanged throws that the current thread is not associated with the Dispatcher; the call must be wrapped in InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged).
- ui-dotnet-08 | ui-dotnet | middle | multi | Which of the listed events make a ComponentBase-derived Blazor component re-render without an explicit StateHasChanged call? | ComponentBase re-renders automatically after its own event handlers complete, after receiving new parameters from a re-rendering parent and after lifecycle methods finish; a field changed by a timer or by an injected service raising its own event does not re-render the component on its own.
- ui-dotnet-09 | ui-dotnet | middle | single | A button bound to a custom ICommand stays disabled after the condition checked by CanExecute becomes true; what is missing? | The bound control queries CanExecute only when the command raises CanExecuteChanged, so the command must raise that event when its condition changes.
- ui-dotnet-10 | ui-dotnet | middle | open | How does BindingContext flow through a .NET MAUI page, and what goes wrong when a child element or a DataTemplate item has a different context than the developer expects? | BindingContext is inherited down the visual tree unless a child sets its own, and inside a DataTemplate the context is the collection item, so a binding to a page-level command needs an explicit Source (for example a relative source or x:Reference) instead of the inherited context.
- ui-dotnet-11 | ui-dotnet | middle | situation | A Blazor app shows a cart counter in the layout header that must update when a product page several levels away adds an item; how do you design the state sharing? | Use a scoped state container service that holds the cart and raises a change event; subscribing components call InvokeAsync(StateHasChanged) in the handler and unsubscribe in Dispose, because a mutable service does not trigger re-rendering by itself and cascading parameters suit values flowing down one subtree rather than sibling updates.
- ui-dotnet-12 | ui-dotnet | senior | open | Why can removing or reordering items in a Blazor list without @key show stale input values or reset the wrong child component, and how does @key fix it? | Without @key the render-tree diff matches elements and components by position in the sequence, so state is reused for a different item; @key makes the diff match by the key value, preserving or recreating the right element at some extra diff cost.
- ui-dotnet-13 | ui-dotnet | senior | situation | A WPF ListBox bound to 100,000 items takes seconds to open and uses a lot of memory after it was moved into a StackPanel inside a ScrollViewer; how do you diagnose and fix it? | UI virtualization in VirtualizingStackPanel works only when the panel gets a constrained viewport and item scrolling; placing the list in an unbounded StackPanel or ScrollViewer, setting CanContentScroll to false or grouping without virtualization support makes WPF create a container for every item, so the fix is to restore a constrained layout and keep virtualization and container recycling enabled.
- ui-dotnet-14 | ui-dotnet | senior | open | Describe how WPF renders a window: what the retained visual tree is, what the UI thread and the render thread each do, and why a long synchronous handler freezes input while the window can still be redrawn. | WPF is retained mode: the UI thread owns DispatcherObjects, processes input and layout and updates the visual tree, while a separate render thread composes that tree to the screen, so blocking the UI thread stops input and layout updates but not composition of what is already in the tree.
- teamwork-01 | teamwork | junior | single | Asks why teams ask authors to split a large change into small, focused pull requests. | Small, self-contained changes are reviewed faster and more thoroughly, merge with fewer conflicts and are easier to roll back. Smaller diffs are not mainly preferred for cosmetic reasons.
- teamwork-02 | teamwork | middle | open | Asks how a reviewer should write comments so the author can tell which ones block the merge and which are optional. | Label non-blocking comments explicitly (for example Nit or Optional), explain the reason behind each request, and comment on the code rather than the person.
- teamwork-03 | teamwork | middle | situation | A manager asks for a firm delivery date for a task whose requirements and integration points are still unclear; what do you answer? | Give a range with explicit assumptions instead of a single number, and propose a short time-boxed investigation to reduce the uncertainty before committing to a date.
- teamwork-04 | teamwork | middle | multi | Asks which statements about the Definition of Done are true according to the Scrum Guide. | The Definition of Done is a shared quality commitment for the Increment, and work that does not meet it cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review. It is not a per-task checklist that each developer chooses for themselves.
- teamwork-05 | teamwork | senior | situation | Minutes after a deploy, error rates spike and the team in the incident call starts debating the root cause in the code; what do you do? | Restore service first by rolling back or otherwise mitigating, with one clear incident lead and communication owner. The root cause analysis comes after users are no longer affected.
- teamwork-06 | teamwork | senior | situation | Two senior engineers have blocked each other's pull requests for a week over competing design approaches; how do you resolve it? | Move from comment threads to a synchronous discussion, judge the options against agreed criteria or data, and escalate to a named decision maker if there is still no consensus. Once the decision is recorded, both commit to it.
- teamwork-07 | teamwork | senior | open | Asks how a senior engineer should mentor a junior whose pull requests need heavy changes, instead of rewriting the code themselves. | Let the mentee keep ownership of the change. Guide them with questions and feedback on their reasoning, pair on the hard parts, and grow the scope of their tasks step by step. Rewriting the code for them removes the learning.
- teamwork-08 | teamwork | lead | situation | After an outage caused by an engineer running a script against production, a manager wants the person's name in the postmortem report; how do you run the postmortem? | Keep the postmortem blameless: focus on the systemic gaps that let one action cause an outage and turn them into owned action items. Blame makes people hide information in future incidents.
- teamwork-09 | teamwork | lead | situation | Pull requests on your team routinely wait several days for a first review and developers start bypassing it; what changes do you make? | Treat review response time as a team priority with an agreed turnaround, spread reviewing across the team and push for smaller changes. Speed improves without lowering the review bar.
- teamwork-10 | teamwork | lead | situation | Only one engineer understands a business-critical module and is about to go on long leave; how do you reduce the risk? | Spread the knowledge on purpose: pairing and rotating work on the module, written documentation of its decisions, and gradually moving ownership to others. This is a team risk, not the individual's fault.
- teamwork-11 | teamwork | lead | situation | Halfway to a committed release date you see the feature will not be ready; what do you do and with whom? | Tell stakeholders as early as possible and offer explicit trade-offs between scope and date. Do not hide the slip behind silent overtime or cut quality.
- teamwork-12 | teamwork | lead | open | Asks how a tech lead should argue for time to pay down technical debt with a product owner who only prioritises features. | State the debt in business cost such as slower delivery, incident rate and risk, and agree on a steady share of capacity for it instead of asking for a large rewrite.
- teamwork-13 | teamwork | architect | open | Asks what architecture decision records are for and how to keep them useful across teams and years. | An ADR captures the context, the decision and its consequences, so later teams understand why a choice was made. Accepted records are not rewritten; a new ADR supersedes the old one when the decision changes.
- teamwork-14 | teamwork | architect | single | Asks which conclusion about organising teams follows from Conway's law when several teams own a set of services. | A system's structure mirrors its organisation's communication structure, so team ownership boundaries must be designed together with service boundaries. Otherwise the architecture drifts toward the org chart.
- behavioral-01 | behavioral | junior | situation | You have been stuck on a task for two days and feel embarrassed to ask anyone; what do you do now and what would you do differently next time? | Timebox solo effort, then ask early with a short summary of the goal, what you tried and where you are stuck, because silent struggle hides a schedule risk from the team.
- behavioral-02 | behavioral | junior | single | You realise that your merge has broken the shared test environment that other developers rely on; which first action is best? | Tell the affected people immediately and revert or roll back your change first, before investigating the root cause quietly or trying to fix it unnoticed.
- behavioral-03 | behavioral | junior | open | A ticket you picked up can be read two different ways; what do you do before writing code? | Restate your understanding and assumptions to the requester, ideally as written acceptance criteria, and get confirmation instead of guessing and building one interpretation.
- behavioral-04 | behavioral | middle | situation | Your manager asks you to skip writing tests so a feature ships by Friday; how do you respond? | Make the trade-off explicit, offer to cut scope rather than quality, and if the shortcut is still chosen, record it as deliberate debt with an agreed payback, leaving the risk decision to its owner.
- behavioral-05 | behavioral | middle | situation | Two stakeholders each ask you directly to do their task first and both call it urgent; what do you do? | Do not pick a winner or split your effort in secret; make the conflict visible and let the person accountable for priority, such as the product owner, decide the order.
- behavioral-06 | behavioral | middle | open | An interviewer asks you to describe a project or task that failed; what makes a strong answer? | A strong answer names a concrete situation, your own part in it, what you did, the outcome and what you changed afterwards, and does not blame others.
- behavioral-07 | behavioral | middle | situation | The team chose a technical approach you argued against, and now you are asked to implement it; what do you do? | State your concerns once with evidence and get them recorded, then commit fully to the chosen approach and agree on a signal that would trigger a revisit, instead of sabotaging or reopening the decision repeatedly.
- behavioral-08 | behavioral | senior | situation | Product asks you to implement a feature that collects user data without clear consent; what do you do? | Raise the concern in writing to the people who own the decision, citing the user harm and legal risk, and escalate if needed, rather than silently complying or silently refusing.
- behavioral-09 | behavioral | senior | open | You are the only person who understands a business-critical subsystem; what would you do about it? | Treat being the single point of knowledge as a risk and spread it deliberately through pairing, written runbooks and handing tasks in that area to others before it is urgent.
- behavioral-10 | behavioral | senior | open | You are asked whether the team should adopt a popular new library that everyone is talking about; how do you decide? | Judge it against the concrete problem with a timeboxed spike and explicit exit criteria, weighing maintenance health, licence and migration cost, not popularity.
- behavioral-11 | behavioral | lead | situation | Your team has worked overtime for several sprints in a row to hit dates; what do you do as the lead? | Treat chronic overtime as a planning failure and negotiate scope or dates with stakeholders to restore a sustainable pace, because heroics hide the real capacity and lead to burnout and defects.
- behavioral-12 | behavioral | lead | open | How do you decide how much of the team's time goes to paying down technical debt instead of new features? | Tie debt work to its measured cost on delivery, focus on areas of the code that change often, and reserve steady capacity instead of waiting for a large cleanup project.
- behavioral-13 | behavioral | lead | single | Management asks you to report lines of code or story points per developer as a productivity ranking; which response is best? | Push back on individual output metrics because they get gamed and harm collaboration, and offer team-level delivery and outcome metrics such as the DORA measures instead.
- behavioral-14 | behavioral | architect | situation | An executive wants to rewrite a ten-year-old core system from scratch on a new stack within a year; how do you respond? | Argue for incremental replacement behind stable interfaces, as in the strangler fig approach, with business value delivered at each step, because a big-bang rewrite loses embedded knowledge and freezes delivery for a long time.
